title: How to Start a Vegetable Garden in a Raised Bed
hook: A raised bed is the easiest way to grow vegetables, even with poor soil, a bad back or a small yard. You control the soil, the weeds stay low, and the harvest is bigger. In seven steps, you'll build and plant your first raised bed this weekend. No experience is needed, and you can finish the build in an afternoon, and what to do when plants struggle.
intro: Raised beds warm up faster in spring, drain better, and are easier to look after than a garden dug into the ground. You can build one from simple wooden boards in an afternoon. The secret to success is a good location, a well-built frame, and a rich soil mix. We'll go through each stage, from choosing the site to planting your first seedlings, with tips to avoid the common beginner problems. A raised bed also lets you start growing on poor ground, where digging would be hard work.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. Untreated boards, such as cedar or pine, about four feet wide, and eight feet long, for a standard bed. Screws and a drill, and a tape measure. Plain cardboard. A mix of good topsoil and compost, and a watering can or hose. And finally the fun part, seedlings or seeds of the vegetables you love.
heroImagePrompt: A wooden raised garden bed filled with healthy vegetable seedlings in rich dark soil, a watering can nearby, morning sunlight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Choose a sunny, level spot
steps.narration: Step one. Most vegetables need six to eight hours of direct sunlight each day. Watch your yard for a day, and choose the sunniest area, close to a water source. The ground should be roughly level, and away from large tree roots. A good size for your first bed is four feet wide and eight feet long, or about one point two by two point four metres. Four feet wide means you can reach the middle from either side without stepping on the soil. If you have only a balcony, a deep container works in much the same way, with the same rules about sun.
steps.tip: Four feet wide is reachable from both sides
steps.mistake: Building a bed in the shade
steps.imagePrompt: A sunny level patch of lawn in a backyard marked out with string for a garden bed, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Build the frame
steps.narration: Step two. Cut your boards to length, or ask the store to cut them. Use untreated cedar or pine, which is safe for growing food. Avoid old railroad ties or boards treated with strong chemicals. Screw the corners together, using short posts inside the corners for strength, and make the bed ten to twelve inches, or about thirty centimetres, deep. Set the frame in place, and check it with a level. Press it gently into the ground so it sits steady. Corner posts also give you something to attach plant supports or netting to later in the season.
steps.imagePrompt: A person screwing together wooden boards into a rectangular raised bed frame on a lawn, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Line the bottom with cardboard
steps.narration: Step three. Remove any large weeds from inside the frame. Then cover the ground with a layer of plain cardboard, with staples and tape removed, overlapping the edges so that no gaps remain. Wet it down with water. The cardboard blocks light so grass and weeds underneath die off, and it breaks down over time, letting roots reach the soil below. This saves you from digging and cuts down on weeding in the first season. A thick layer of newspaper will also work, if you don't have cardboard handy. Wet it as you go so that it stays in place.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps where weeds can push through
steps.imagePrompt: Flattened brown cardboard laid inside an empty wooden raised bed frame on grass, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Fill with a rich soil mix
steps.narration: Step four. Fill the bed with a mix of about half good-quality topsoil and half compost. This gives you a soil that is rich in nutrients, but still drains well. You can add a few handfuls of perlite or coarse sand to lighten it. Fill the bed to within an inch or two of the top, then rake it level. Water it well and let it settle for a day or two. Top it up if the soil sinks, which it usually does. Fill slowly in layers, and water each layer lightly. This helps remove air pockets that would sink later.
steps.mistake: Filling with plain garden soil only
steps.imagePrompt: Dark rich soil and compost being shoveled into a wooden raised bed, wheelbarrow beside it, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Plan and plant
steps.narration: Step five. Decide what to grow, and check the spacing on the seed packet or plant label. Put taller plants, like tomatoes and beans, on the north side, so they don't shade smaller plants. Plant lettuce, radishes and herbs near the edges for easy picking. Use a trowel to make holes, set the seedlings in at the same depth they sat in their pots, firm the soil, and water in. A simple grid, one plant per square foot, helps you avoid overcrowding. Mark each row with a label, so you remember what is where. Water the seedlings gently right after planting.
steps.tip: Tall plants on the north side
steps.imagePrompt: Hands planting small vegetable seedlings in neat rows in a raised bed with a trowel, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Water and mulch
steps.narration: Step six. Raised beds drain quickly, so they need regular watering, especially in summer. Aim for about one inch of water per week, delivered deeply, at the base of the plants and in the morning. A soaker hose or drip line saves time and water. Spread two inches of straw or shredded leaves over the soil, keeping it a little away from the stems. Mulch keeps the soil cool and moist, and reduces weeds by a surprising amount. In very hot weather, check the soil every day. A finger pushed in two inches shows you how dry it is.
steps.tip: Water at the base, in the morning
steps.imagePrompt: Golden straw mulch spread around healthy vegetable plants in a raised bed with a soaker hose, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Maintain and replant
steps.narration: Step seven. Visit your bed a few times a week. Pull weeds while they are small, look under leaves for pests, and harvest regularly, because picking encourages more. When a crop finishes, plant something new in its place, like a fall crop of kale or spinach. At the end of the season, add a couple of inches of compost to the soil to replenish the nutrients. Your raised bed will get better each year. Keep a simple notebook, with what you planted, and when, so that next year you can rotate crops.
steps.mistake: Letting finished plants sit and rot
steps.imagePrompt: Hands harvesting fresh lettuce and tomatoes from a wooden raised bed into a basket, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: NOT WORKING?
bonus.title: When plants struggle
bonus.narration: Yellow leaves often mean too much water, or soil that is short of nutrients. Push a finger two inches into the soil to see which. If it is soggy, water less. If it is dry and the plants look pale, mix in some compost, or a balanced fertilizer used as the label says. If leaves have holes, check under them in the evening, and pick off slugs and caterpillars by hand.
bonus.tip: Check the soil before you act
bonus.imagePrompt: A gardener's hand turning over a green tomato leaf with a few small holes and pale patches, a raised bed with healthy plants blurred behind. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Sunny backyard garden, natural light. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: GO FURTHER
bonus.title: Get more from the same space
bonus.narration: Once the bed is running, a few tricks make it more productive. Grow climbers like beans, peas and cucumbers up a trellis, which saves floor space. Sow fast crops like radishes between slow ones like tomatoes, and harvest them before the big plants need the room. Sow lettuce every two weeks, so you never get everything at once. A simple hoop covered with garden fabric protects young plants from light frost.
bonus.imagePrompt: A wooden raised garden bed with green bean plants climbing a tall trellis at the back and rows of lettuce and radishes in front. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Sunny backyard garden, natural light. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: KEEP IT HEALTHY
bonus.title: Keep the soil healthy
bonus.narration: Avoid stepping on the bed, because compacted soil holds less air. Do not work it when it is very wet, since it clumps and sets hard. Water at the base of the plants, so leaves stay dry, which helps prevent many fungal diseases. Remove diseased plants, and throw them in the trash instead of the compost pile. Keep the surface covered with mulch, so bare soil never dries out and washes away.
bonus.imagePrompt: Two hands cupped around a handful of dark, crumbly, rich garden soil above a raised bed, mulch visible on the surface. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Sunny backyard garden, natural light. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, placing the bed in too much shade. Even the best soil can't make up for a lack of sun. Second, using poor soil, or filling the bed with plain garden dirt, which compacts and drains badly. And third, forgetting to water. Raised beds dry out faster than the ground, so check them often. Get the sun, the soil and the water right, and the rest is easy. A little planning before you build saves a lot of work afterward.
items: Filling with poor or compacted soil

recap.narration: Let's recap. Choose a sunny, level spot. Build a frame from untreated wood. Line the bottom with cardboard. Fill with half topsoil and half compost. Plan and plant. Water deeply and add mulch. And maintain your bed and replant as crops finish. Seven steps, one weekend, and vegetables growing at your doorstep. Bonus sections cover what to do when plants struggle, how to get more from the same space, and how to keep the soil healthy.
items: Fill with a rich soil mix

outro: That's how you start a vegetable garden in a raised bed. If you're ready to build one, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments what you plan to grow first, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow.

metadata.title: How to Start a Vegetable Garden in a Raised Bed
metadata.description:
Want to grow vegetables with less work? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to start a vegetable garden in a raised bed: choose a sunny spot, build a frame from untreated wood, line the bottom with cardboard, fill with a topsoil and compost mix, plan and plant your seedlings, water and mulch, and maintain the bed through the season. A beginner-friendly guide for small yards and poor soil.

You'll need: untreated wood boards, screws and a drill, cardboard, compost and topsoil, seedlings or seeds.
